name: Nice · French Riviera
tagline: Blue bay, old town and the Riviera by train
summary: The capital of the Côte d'Azur, with a pebble beach, an Italian-feeling old town and excellent art museums. The coastal train makes it the best base for Monaco, Èze, Villefranche and Antibes.
seasonNote: July and August are hot, crowded and expensive; February has the Carnival; winter is mild and sunny.
arrival: Nice airport is 7 km west; tram line 2 reaches the centre in 25 minutes. TGV trains from Paris take about 6 hours.
gettingAround: Walk the centre and use the trams. Coastal trains and bus 600 run to Villefranche, Èze-sur-Mer and Monaco.
cashTip: Cards and contactless are accepted nearly everywhere; keep coins for market stalls.
foodTip: Niçoise street food: socca (chickpea pancake), pissaladière, pan bagnat and a true salade niçoise without cooked vegetables.
buyTip: Olive oil, candied fruit and lavender soap from the Cours Saleya and old town shops.
baseArea: Between the old town and Place Masséna, or the Carré d'Or

connections.note: Frequent flights; the TGV takes about 6 hours.
TGV or regional train via Marseille.

items.name: Promenade des Anglais
items.summary: A 7 km seafront walk along the Baie des Anges, lined with blue chairs and Belle Époque hotels.
items.expect: The beach is pebbles; private beach clubs charge for loungers.
items.tip: Walk it early or at dusk, and bring water shoes to swim.
items.why: The image of Nice.
flow: Walk east to the old town and Castle Hill.

items.name: Vieux Nice and Cours Saleya market
items.summary: Ochre lanes, baroque churches and a daily flower and food market.
items.expect: The food market runs Tuesday to Sunday mornings; Monday is antiques.
items.tip: Come before 10 am, then wander the lanes behind.
items.why: The most atmospheric quarter on the Riviera.
flow: Lanes north to Place Rossetti for ice cream.

items.name: Castle Hill
items.summary: A wooded park on the site of the old citadel, with the classic view over the bay and the rooftops.
items.expect: About 200 steps, or a free lift from the seafront.
items.tip: Go for sunset from the terrace by the waterfall.
items.why: The best view in the city, for free.
flow: Stairs or lift from the east end of the promenade.
Viewpoints on both the bay and the port side.

items.name: Musée Matisse
items.summary: A red villa in an olive grove holding work from every period of Matisse's life in Nice.
items.expect: Closed on Tuesdays; a bus ride uphill.
items.tip: Add the Roman ruins and the monastery garden next door.
items.why: Matisse lived and worked here for nearly 40 years.

items.name: Musée National Marc Chagall
items.summary: A museum built around Chagall's cycle of 17 large biblical paintings.
items.expect: Small and calm; closed on Tuesdays.
items.tip: Sit in the concert hall to see the blue stained glass.
items.why: The largest public collection of Chagall's work.
flow: The main hall, then the garden cafe.

items.name: Èze village
items.summary: A medieval village on a rock 430 metres above the sea, topped by a cactus garden.
items.expect: Steep lanes and tour groups at midday.
items.tip: Take bus 82 or 602 up, and walk the Nietzsche path down to the station if your knees allow.
items.why: The most dramatic view on the coast.
flow: Climb to the exotic garden at the top.

items.name: Monaco
items.summary: The tiny principality of the casino, the palace and a harbour full of superyachts.
items.expect: Hilly, with public lifts; pricey for food.
items.tip: See the old town on the rock and the Oceanographic Museum, then Casino Square.
items.why: A different country 25 minutes away by train.
flow: The Rock in the morning, Monte Carlo in the afternoon.

items.name: Villefranche-sur-Mer
items.summary: A pastel fishing town on a deep bay with a sandy beach.
items.expect: Busy on summer weekends.
items.tip: The beach is two minutes from the train station.
items.why: A better swim than Nice, 7 minutes away.
flow: Beach, then lunch on the quay.

items.name: Chez Pipo
items.summary: A socca specialist since 1923, baking chickpea pancakes in a wood oven.
items.expect: A queue and shared tables.
items.tip: Eat the socca hot with black pepper and a glass of rosé.
items.why: The reference for Nice's favourite snack.
flow: Socca, pissaladière and a salad to share.

items.name: La Merenda
items.summary: A tiny bistro with stools and a blackboard of classic Niçoise dishes.
items.expect: Two sittings, tight seating and a short menu.
items.tip: Book online for the first sitting.
items.why: The most faithful traditional cooking in the city.
flow: Stuffed vegetables, then daube or tripe.

items.name: Chez Acchiardo
items.summary: A family-run old-town restaurant open since 1927.
items.expect: Closed at weekends; lively and full of regulars.
items.tip: Reserve, and order the house ravioli.
items.why: Generous local cooking at fair prices.
flow: Ravioli à la daube, then a tart.

name: Lyon
tagline: France's food capital between two rivers
summary: A handsome city of Renaissance lanes, Roman theatres and hidden passageways, best known for its bouchons. Two days cover the old town, Fourvière hill and a lot of eating.
seasonNote: The Festival of Lights around 8 December draws millions; August is hot and many restaurants close.
arrival: TGV trains from Paris take 2 hours to Part-Dieu or Perrache. The Rhônexpress tram links the airport in 30 minutes.
gettingAround: Metro, trams and two funiculars up Fourvière; the centre is walkable.
cashTip: Cards everywhere; some market stalls want cash.
foodTip: Eat in a bouchon: quenelles, saucisson brioché, salade lyonnaise, then praline tart.
buyTip: Silk scarves from Croix-Rousse workshops; pink praline sweets.

items.name: Vieux Lyon and the traboules
items.summary: One of Europe's largest Renaissance quarters, threaded with covered passageways between streets.
items.expect: Traboules are behind ordinary doors; push the ones with a small plaque and keep quiet, as people live there.
items.tip: Try 54 Rue Saint-Jean for the longest passage.
items.why: A UNESCO World Heritage site and the heart of the city.
flow: Cathedral Saint-Jean, Rue Saint-Jean, then the courtyards.

items.name: Basilica of Notre-Dame de Fourvière
items.summary: A white hilltop basilica covered inside with gold mosaics, with a terrace over the whole city.
items.expect: Free entry; rooftop tours in season.
items.tip: Ride the funicular up and walk down through the rose garden.
items.why: The city's landmark and its best panorama.

items.name: Roman theatres of Fourvière
items.summary: A 10,000-seat Roman theatre and a smaller odeon, with the Lugdunum museum built into the hillside.
items.expect: The theatres are free; the museum is ticketed.
items.tip: Summer evenings bring the Nuits de Fourvière concerts.
items.why: Lyon was the capital of Roman Gaul.
flow: Sit in the theatre, then the museum.

items.name: Musée des Confluences
items.summary: A science and anthropology museum in a glass-and-steel building where the Rhône meets the Saône.
items.expect: Closed on Mondays; good for children.
items.tip: Walk to the tip of the peninsula afterwards.
items.why: A striking building with well-told exhibitions.
flow: Origins hall, then the roof terrace.

items.name: Museum of Fine Arts
items.wiki: Museum of Fine Arts of Lyon
items.summary: One of France's best art museums outside Paris, in a former abbey on Place des Terreaux.
items.expect: Closed on Tuesdays.
items.tip: The cloister garden is free and makes a quiet break.
items.why: From Egyptian antiquities to Monet and Picasso.
flow: Paintings on the second floor, then the garden.

items.name: La Croix-Rousse
items.summary: The hill of the silk weavers, with tall workshop buildings, murals and a daily market.
items.expect: Steep staircases on the slopes.
items.tip: See the Mur des Canuts mural and take the Cour des Voraces traboule downhill.
items.why: The most lived-in, village-like part of Lyon.
flow: Market, mural, then down the slopes to Terreaux.

items.name: Parc de la Tête d'Or
items.summary: A large park with a lake, botanical greenhouses and a free zoo.
items.expect: Busy on sunny weekends.
items.tip: Rent a boat or visit the rose garden in June.
items.why: The city's green lung.

items.name: Les Halles de Lyon Paul Bocuse
items.summary: A covered market of about 50 top-quality stalls with counters for oysters, cheese and charcuterie.
items.expect: Closed Monday; Sunday is morning only.
items.tip: Go late morning and eat at the counters.
items.why: The showcase of Lyon's food.
flow: Cheese from Mère Richard, charcuterie from Sibilia, then oysters.

items.name: Daniel et Denise Saint-Jean
items.summary: A certified bouchon run by chef Joseph Viola, with checked tablecloths and classic dishes.
items.expect: Rich, generous plates.
items.tip: Order the pâté en croûte, a world-champion recipe.
items.why: The most reliable bouchon in the old town.
flow: Pâté en croûte, quenelle, praline tart.

items.name: Café Comptoir Abel
items.summary: One of the oldest bouchons in the city, with wood-panelled rooms unchanged for a century.
items.expect: Large portions; an older local crowd.
items.tip: The quenelle is the house speciality.
items.why: For the room as much as the cooking.

name: Bordeaux
tagline: Golden stone city in the middle of the vineyards
summary: An elegant 18th-century city on the Garonne and the capital of the world's most famous wine region. Spend a day or two in town, one in Saint-Émilion and one at the Dune of Pilat.
seasonNote: Harvest in September and October is the best time for vineyards; many châteaux close on Sundays and in August.
arrival: TGV trains from Paris take 2 hours 10 minutes. The airport is 12 km west, linked by tram A.
gettingAround: The centre is flat and largely car-free; use the trams and bikes. Trains run to Saint-Émilion and Arcachon.
foodTip: Canelés, oysters from Arcachon with white wine, entrecôte à la bordelaise and duck.
buyTip: Wine, of course, and canelés from Baillardran or La Toque Cuivrée.
baseArea: The old town between the Grand Théâtre and Saint-Pierre

items.name: Place de la Bourse and the Miroir d'eau
items.summary: A grand 18th-century square reflected in the world's largest water mirror.
items.expect: The water runs from spring to autumn, alternating mist and reflection.
items.tip: Come at dusk when the façades are lit.
items.why: The classic view of Bordeaux.
flow: Tram C to Place de la Bourse.
Walk the quays north or south.

items.name: La Cité du Vin
items.summary: An interactive museum of wine cultures around the world, ending with a glass on the top-floor belvedere.
items.expect: Two to three hours; a tasting is included in the ticket.
items.tip: Book a timed ticket online and go in the morning.
items.why: The best introduction before visiting vineyards.
flow: Tram B to La Cité du Vin.

items.name: Bordeaux Cathedral and Tour Pey-Berland
items.summary: A Gothic cathedral with a separate bell tower you can climb for a rooftop view.
items.expect: 231 narrow steps up the tower.
items.tip: Climb the tower rather than only seeing the cathedral.
items.why: The best high view of the old town.
flow: Tram A or B to Hôtel de Ville.

items.name: Old town walk: Grosse Cloche to Saint-Pierre
items.summary: Medieval gates, the long shopping street of Rue Sainte-Catherine and the small squares of Saint-Pierre.
items.expect: Mostly pedestrian; lively in the evening.
items.tip: Start at the Grosse Cloche bell gate and finish with a drink on Place du Parlement.
items.why: The centre is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
flow: Rue Sainte-Catherine, Porte Cailhau, Place du Parlement.

items.name: Saint-Émilion
items.summary: A medieval wine village above its vineyards, with an underground church cut from the rock.
items.expect: Steep cobbled lanes; the monolithic church is by guided tour only.
items.tip: Book one château visit and the underground tour, and leave time to wander.
items.why: The prettiest wine town in France, and a UNESCO World Heritage site.
flow: Train from Bordeaux, 35 minutes, then a 20-minute walk.
Village, underground church, a château tasting.
items.book: A few days ahead for châteaux

items.name: Dune of Pilat
items.summary: Europe's tallest sand dune, over 100 metres high, between pine forest and the Atlantic.
items.expect: A stiff climb, with stairs installed in season; windy on top.
items.tip: Train to Arcachon, then bus 3; stay for sunset and eat oysters in Arcachon.
items.why: A startling piece of landscape an hour from the city.
flow: Train to Arcachon, 50 minutes, then the bus.
Climb, walk the ridge, run down the sea side.

items.name: Marché des Capucins
items.summary: The city's main covered market, with oyster bars and small counters among the stalls.
items.expect: Mornings only; closed Monday; busiest at weekends.
items.tip: Have oysters and a glass of white at Chez Jean-Mi.
items.why: Where Bordeaux has its weekend brunch.
flow: Oysters, then a canelé and coffee.

items.name: La Tupina
items.summary: A country-style restaurant where meat roasts over an open fire in the dining room.
items.expect: Hearty south-western cooking; not cheap.
items.tip: The weekday lunch menu is the best value.
items.why: The reference for the cooking of the south-west.
flow: Roast chicken or duck with chips fried in duck fat.

items.name: Le Petit Commerce
items.summary: A busy seafood bistro spread across both sides of a narrow lane.
items.expect: Noisy, quick and popular.
items.tip: Choose from the day's fish on the blackboard.
items.why: Fresh Atlantic fish at reasonable prices in the old town.

name: Strasbourg · Alsace
tagline: Half-timbered canals and a pink cathedral
summary: A French city with a German accent, on an island ringed by canals. See the cathedral and Petite France in a day, then take the train to Colmar and the wine villages. December brings France's oldest Christmas market.
seasonNote: The Christmas market runs from late November to 24 December and hotel prices double; January to March is cold and quiet.
arrival: TGV trains from Paris take 1 hour 50 minutes. The small airport is 10 minutes away by train.
gettingAround: The island centre is walkable; trams cover the rest. Trains reach Colmar in 30 minutes.
cashTip: Cards everywhere; cash helps at Christmas market stalls.
foodTip: Tarte flambée (flammekueche), choucroute garnie, baeckeoffe and kougelhopf, with Riesling or Gewürztraminer.
buyTip: Christmas decorations, Alsace wine, gingerbread and Soufflenheim pottery.
baseArea: On the Grande Île, near the cathedral or Petite France

connections.note: Frequent TGVs from Gare de l'Est.

items.name: Strasbourg Cathedral
items.summary: A pink sandstone Gothic cathedral with a single spire that was the world's tallest building for two centuries.
items.expect: The astronomical clock performs at 12:30; the platform is 330 steps up.
items.tip: Visit early, then return for the clock, and climb the platform on a clear day.
items.why: One of the great Gothic buildings of Europe.

items.name: Petite France
items.summary: The old tanners' quarter of half-timbered houses leaning over canals and locks.
items.expect: Crowded at midday and all through December.
items.tip: Walk it before 9 am or at dusk.
items.why: The picture-postcard corner of Alsace.
flow: Follow the river from the cathedral.
Place Benjamin-Zix, the locks, then the covered bridges.

items.name: Ponts Couverts and Barrage Vauban
items.summary: Three medieval bridges with towers, seen best from the roof terrace of a 17th-century dam.
items.expect: The terrace is free.
items.tip: Go up at sunset for the view back to the cathedral.
items.why: The best free viewpoint in the city.
flow: Walk through the dam and up to its roof.

items.name: Palais Rohan
items.summary: An 18th-century bishops' palace housing three museums: fine arts, decorative arts and archaeology.
items.expect: Closed on Tuesdays.
items.tip: If short of time, choose the decorative arts apartments.
items.why: A small Versailles beside the cathedral.

items.name: Christkindelsmärik
items.summary: France's oldest Christmas market, held since 1570, spread over a dozen squares.
items.expect: Late November to 24 December only; very crowded at weekends, with security checks on the bridges.
items.tip: Go on a weekday and see the great tree on Place Kléber after dark.
items.why: The reason Strasbourg calls itself the capital of Christmas.
flow: Place Broglie, then Place de la Cathédrale.
Finish at Place Kléber with mulled wine.

items.name: European Parliament
items.wiki: Seat of the European Parliament in Strasbourg
items.summary: The glass home of the European Parliament, open for free visits with a multimedia exhibition.
items.expect: Bring photo ID; plenary weeks need advance booking.
items.tip: Combine with a walk in the Parc de l'Orangerie.
items.why: A look inside one of Europe's capitals.

items.name: Colmar and the Alsace wine villages
items.summary: A storybook town of canals and painted houses, gateway to villages like Riquewihr and Eguisheim.
items.expect: 30 minutes by train; the villages need a bus, tour or car.
items.tip: See Little Venice and the Isenheim Altarpiece, then take bus 106 to Riquewihr.
items.why: The prettiest stretch of the Alsace wine route.
flow: Old town and Unterlinden Museum, then a village.

items.name: Maison Kammerzell
items.summary: A restaurant in an ornately carved 15th-century house on the cathedral square.
items.expect: Touristy but handsome; several floors of dining rooms.
items.tip: Order the choucroute with three fish, the house speciality.
items.why: The most famous building in Strasbourg after the cathedral.
flow: Choucroute and a glass of Riesling.

items.name: Chez Yvonne
items.summary: A classic winstub, a wood-panelled Alsatian wine tavern, open since 1873.
items.expect: Close-set tables and big plates.
items.tip: Book ahead, especially in December.
items.why: The archetype of the Strasbourg tavern.
flow: Onion tart, then baeckeoffe or ham knuckle.

items.name: Binchstub
items.summary: A small, modern tavern devoted to tarte flambée with seasonal toppings.
items.expect: Tiny and full; book or come early.
items.tip: Share two savoury tartes and one sweet.
items.why: The best flammekueche in the centre.
flow: Classic tarte first, then a seasonal one.

name: Avignon · Provence
tagline: City of the popes and gateway to Provence
summary: A walled city on the Rhône that was the seat of the popes in the 14th century. It is the best rail base for Provence: the Pont du Gard, Arles, Les Baux and the Luberon villages are all within an hour.
seasonNote: Lavender blooms from late June to mid-July; the July theatre festival fills every bed; the mistral wind can blow hard in winter and spring.
arrival: TGV trains from Paris take 2 hours 40 minutes to Avignon TGV station, 5 minutes by shuttle train from the centre. Marseille airport is an hour away.
gettingAround: The walled city is walkable. Trains run to Arles and Nîmes; buses reach the Pont du Gard; the Luberon needs a car or tour.
foodTip: Provençal cooking: daube, ratatouille, tapenade, goat's cheese and Côtes du Rhône wine; calissons for a sweet.
buyTip: Olive oil, lavender, Provençal fabrics and Châteauneuf-du-Pape wine.
baseArea: Inside the walls, near Place de l'Horloge

connections.note: Direct trains from Avignon TGV or via Nîmes.

items.name: Palais des Papes
items.summary: The largest Gothic palace in Europe, home to seven popes in the 14th century.
items.expect: Vast bare halls brought to life by a tablet guide; many stairs.
items.tip: Buy the combined ticket with the bridge and go at opening.
items.why: A UNESCO World Heritage site and the reason Avignon exists as it does.
flow: Follow the tablet route to the rooftop terrace.

items.name: Pont Saint-Bénézet
items.summary: The broken medieval bridge of the song 'Sur le pont d'Avignon', with four arches left in the Rhône.
items.expect: A short visit; the best view of it is free, from the riverbank or the Rocher des Doms.
items.tip: Take the free river shuttle to Île de la Barthelasse for the photo.
items.why: The symbol of the city.
flow: Out along the bridge to the chapel.

items.name: Rocher des Doms
items.summary: A garden on the rock above the palace with views over the Rhône, the bridge and Mont Ventoux.
items.expect: Free; a duck pond and a cafe.
items.tip: Come at sunset.
items.why: The best view in Avignon.

items.name: Pont du Gard
items.summary: A three-tier Roman aqueduct bridge, 49 metres high, across the Gardon river.
items.expect: A large site with a museum; you can swim in the river below in summer.
items.tip: Take bus 115 from Avignon and bring a swimsuit.
items.why: The most impressive Roman monument in France.
flow: Walk across the lower tier, then down to the river beach.

items.name: Arles
items.summary: A Roman amphitheatre and theatre in the town where Van Gogh painted for a year.
items.expect: 20 minutes by train; a big Saturday market.
items.tip: Buy the monuments pass and follow the Van Gogh easels around town.
items.why: Roman Provence and Van Gogh in one easy day.
flow: Amphitheatre, theatre, Saint-Trophime cloister, the Van Gogh café square.

items.name: Les Baux-de-Provence and Carrières des Lumières
items.summary: A ruined castle on a limestone spur, beside a quarry where paintings are projected onto 14-metre walls.
items.expect: Very busy in summer; parking is the hard part.
items.tip: Book the quarry show online and arrive before 10 am.
items.why: A dramatic village and an immersive art show.
flow: Quarry show first, then the castle.

items.name: Gordes and Sénanque Abbey
items.summary: A stone village stacked on a hillside and a Cistercian abbey fronted by lavender fields.
items.expect: Lavender is in flower from late June to mid-July only; a car or tour is needed.
items.tip: Stop at the viewpoint on the road into Gordes, and add Roussillon's ochre cliffs.
items.why: The Provence of the postcards.
flow: Gordes viewpoint, the abbey, then Roussillon.

items.name: Les Halles d'Avignon
items.summary: A covered market of about 40 stalls behind a wall of living plants.
items.expect: Mornings only; closed Monday.
items.tip: Assemble a picnic, or eat oysters at the counter; chefs give a free demonstration on Saturdays.
items.why: The best of Provence's produce under one roof.
flow: Olives, tapenade, cheese and bread for lunch.

items.name: La Fourchette
items.summary: A long-running bistro with a good-value set menu of Provençal classics.
items.expect: Closed at weekends; popular with locals.
items.tip: Reserve, and order the daube.
items.why: Honest regional cooking near Place de l'Horloge.

items.name: L'Épicerie
items.summary: A terrace restaurant on a cobbled square in front of a Gothic church façade.
items.expect: Outdoor tables in season.
items.tip: Order the Provençal sharing plate.
items.why: One of the prettiest places to eat in town.
